At that time Rezin king of Aram{c} recovered Elath for Aram and drove the Judeans out of Elath. Then Edomites{d} came to Elath and have lived there to this day.
Ahaz sent envoys to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria to say, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the grasp of the king of Aram and the king of Israel, who are attacking me.”
Ahaz took the silver and gold found in Yahweh’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s palace and sent it as a present{e} to the king of Assyria.
The king of Assyria agreed. He marched up against Damascus and captured it, deported its people to Kir,{f} and put Rezin to death.

When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar that was at Damascus. King Ahaz sent Uriah{g} the priest a model of the altar and a detailed plan for building it.
Uriah the priest built the altar exactly as King Ahaz had instructed from Damascus, finishing it before King Ahaz came back from Damascus.
When the king arrived from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached the altar and went up on it.
There he offered up his burnt offering and grain offering, made his drink offering, and dashed against the altar the blood from his fellowship sacrifices.
The bronze altar that stood before Yahweh he moved from the front of the house, from between the new altar and Yahweh’s house, and put it on the north side of his altar.

King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, “On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering, the king’s burnt offering and his grain offering, and the burnt offering of all the people of the land, with their grain offerings and drink offerings. Splash on it all the blood of the burnt offerings and sacrifices. But the bronze altar will be for me to seek guidance.”{h}
Uriah the priest did all that King Ahaz commanded.
King Ahaz cut away the panels of the stands and took the basins off them. He lowered the Sea from the bronze oxen beneath it and placed it on a stone pavement.
Because of the king of Assyria, he removed from Yahweh’s house the covered Sabbath passage{i} that had been built in the house, and the king’s outer entrance.
The rest of the acts of Ahaz, all he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. And Hezekiah{j} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: That is, he offered his son as a burnt sacrifice; compare 3:27 and Deuteronomy 18:10.
Compare Isaiah 7:1–9.
Many interpreters read “Rezin king of Aram” as a later addition and “Aram” as “Edom” in this verse, since the two words look alike in Hebrew.
So the Qere and the Septuagint; the Ketiv reads “Arameans.”
Or “a bribe.”
Kir was the land the Arameans came from (Amos 9:7); its location is unknown.
Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.”
Or “for me to consider.” The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain.
So the Qere; the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “a base for the throne.”
Hezekiah means “Yahweh strengthens.”

verses.text: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned nine years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, though not to the degree of the kings of Israel who came before him.
Shalmaneser{a} king of Assyria marched up against him, and Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute.

But the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea was plotting against him. He had sent envoys to So{b} king of Egypt and had withheld the yearly tribute owed to Assyria’s king. So Assyria’s king seized him and locked him in prison.
Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land. He went up to Samaria and besieged it for three years.

In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria captured Samaria. He carried the Israelites off to Assyria and settled them in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the towns of the Medes.{c}
This happened because the Israelites had sinned against Yahweh their God, the one who led them out of Egypt, out from under the hand of Egypt’s king, Pharaoh. They revered other gods
and lived by the customs of the nations whom Yahweh had driven out before the Israelites, and by the customs that the kings of Israel had introduced.{d}
The Israelites did in secret{e} things that were not right against Yahweh their God. They built high places for themselves in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city.
They set up for themselves sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every leafy tree.
There they burned incense on all the high places, as the nations had done whom Yahweh had carried away before them. They did wicked things that provoked Yahweh to anger.
They served idols,{f} although Yahweh had told them, “You must not do this.”

Yet Yahweh warned Israel and Judah through every prophet and every seer: “Turn back from your evil ways. Keep my commandments and my statutes, in keeping with all the law that I commanded your ancestors and that I sent to you through my servants the prophets.”
But they would not listen. They hardened their necks like their ancestors, who had no faith in Yahweh their God.

They spurned his statutes, the covenant he cut with their fathers, and the solemn warnings he gave them. They went after empty things and became empty themselves,{g} following the nations around them, though Yahweh had commanded them not to act as those nations did.
They abandoned all the commandments of Yahweh their God and made for themselves cast images, two calves. They made an Asherah pole, bowed down to all the host of heaven, and served Baal.
They made their sons and daughters pass through the fire. They practiced divination and sought omens, and they sold themselves to do evil in Yahweh’s sight, provoking him to anger.
So Yahweh was furious with Israel and put them out of his sight. No one remained except the tribe of Judah.
Even Judah did not keep the commandments of Yahweh their God but followed the customs Israel had introduced.
So Yahweh rejected all the descendants of Israel. He humbled them and handed them over to plunderers, until he had thrown them out of his sight.
When he tore Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king. Jeroboam drove Israel away from following Yahweh and made them commit a great sin.
The Israelites kept on in every sin Jeroboam had committed and never turned from them,
until Yahweh removed Israel from his presence, just as he had said through all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria, where they are to this day.

From Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim{h} the Assyrian king brought people and settled them in Samaria’s towns where the Israelites had lived. These newcomers took over Samaria and made their homes in its towns.
When they first settled there, they did not revere Yahweh, so Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them.

It was reported to the king of Assyria: “The nations whom you have exiled and settled in Samaria’s towns are ignorant of the requirements{i} of the god of the land. So he has sent lions among them, and they are killing them, because they do not know what the god of the land requires.”
Then the king of Assyria gave this order: “Send back there one of the priests you deported from there. Let him go and live there and teach them what the god of the land requires.”
So one of the priests whom they had deported from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and he taught them how they should revere Yahweh.
But each nation still made its own gods and set them up in the shrines of the high places that the people of Samaria had made, each nation in the towns where they lived.
Those from Babylon fashioned Succoth-benoth; those from Cuth, Nergal; those from Hamath, Ashima;
and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak. The Sepharvites burned their children in the fire as offerings to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.{j}
They also revered Yahweh, and they appointed from their own number all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who offered sacrifices for them in the shrines of the high places.
So they revered Yahweh but served their own gods, in the manner of the nations from which they had been deported.

To this day they keep their former practices. They do not truly revere Yahweh, nor do they follow the statutes, the rules, the law, or the commandment that Yahweh gave to the descendants of Jacob, whom he named Israel.{k}
Yahweh had made a covenant with them and charged them, “Do not revere other gods, bow down to them, serve them, or sacrifice to them.
Yahweh, who brought you up from the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm, is the one you are to revere. Bow down to him and sacrifice to him.
The statutes, the rules, the law, and the commandment that he wrote for you, you must always be careful to do. Do not revere other gods.
Never forget the covenant I cut with you, and revere no other gods.
Instead, revere Yahweh your God, and he will rescue you from the hand of all your enemies.”
But they would not listen, and they kept on with their former practices.
So these nations revered Yahweh and also served their carved images. Their children and grandchildren do as their ancestors did, to this day.

notes.text: Shalmaneser V reigned in Assyria about 727–722 BC.
So may be the name of a pharaoh, perhaps Osorkon IV, or a place name, Sais, in the Nile delta.
The Septuagint reads “the mountains of the Medes.”
The Hebrew of this clause is awkward; it may mean “and of the kings of Israel, which they practiced.”
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; it may mean “ascribed things falsely to.”
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous term, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Hebrew hebel, “vapor” or “breath,” a play on the idea of worthlessness.
These were cities in Mesopotamia and Syria.
Hebrew mishpat, here “custom” or “required rites.” Likewise in verses 27, 33, 34, and 40.
The names in verses 30–31 refer to deities whose identities are largely uncertain. Nergal was a Mesopotamian god of the underworld.
Verse 34 appears to contradict verses 32–33; it may mean that these people did not worship Yahweh in the way the law required. Jacob was renamed Israel in Genesis 32:28.

verses.text: In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abi{a} daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes, just as his ancestor David had done in everything.

He removed the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah pole. He broke into pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for up to then the Israelites had kept offering incense to it. People called it Nehushtan.{b}
Hezekiah trusted in Yahweh the God of Israel. Among all the kings of Judah, none was like him, whether after him or before him.
He held fast to Yahweh and never stopped following him. He kept the commandments Yahweh had given Moses.
Yahweh was with him, and he succeeded in whatever he undertook. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him.
He struck down the Philistines all the way to Gaza and its borders, from lookout tower to walled town.
In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, the seventh of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it.
At the end of three years they captured it. In Hezekiah’s sixth year, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria fell.
The king of Assyria deported the Israelites to Assyria and settled them in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the towns of the Medes,
because they had not obeyed the voice of Yahweh their God but had broken his covenant, all that Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded. They would neither listen nor obey.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib{c} king of Assyria came up against all the fortified towns of Judah and captured them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent word to the king of Assyria at Lachish: “I have sinned. Pull back from me, and I will bear any burden you lay on me.” So Assyria’s king imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah about 11 tons of silver and about 1 ton of gold.{d}
Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in Yahweh’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s palace.
At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of Yahweh’s temple and from the doorposts that he, Hezekiah king of Judah, had overlaid, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

From Lachish the Assyrian king sent his Tartan, Rab-saris, and Rabshakeh{e} with a large army to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. They went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they took their stand by the channel of the upper pool, which is on the road to the Washer’s Field.
When they called for the king, out to meet them came Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, Shebnah the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Say to Hezekiah, ‘Thus says the great king, Assyria’s king: On what do you base this confidence of yours?
You say you have strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. On whom are you now relying, that you have rebelled against me?
Look, you are leaning on Egypt, a cracked reed for a walking stick, which will stab into the palm of whoever puts weight on it. Such is Egypt’s king Pharaoh to everyone who trusts him.

But if you tell me, “We are relying on Yahweh our God,” is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, telling Judah and Jerusalem, “You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem”?
Now then, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you can put riders on them!
How then can you turn back a single officer, even the least of my master’s servants, when you rely on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?
Besides, is it without Yahweh that I have come up against this place to destroy it? Yahweh himself told me, Go up against this land and destroy it.’ ”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebnah, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Kindly use Aramaic with your servants, since we know that language. Do not address us in Hebrew{f} while the people on the wall can hear.”

But the Rabshakeh replied, “Was it to your master and you alone that my master sent me to say these things? Was it not to the men on the wall, who along with you will be eating their own excrement and drinking their own urine?”{g}
Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew: “Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!
The king says this: ‘Do not let Hezekiah fool you; he cannot save you from his hand.
Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to rely on Yahweh by saying, Yahweh will surely rescue us; Assyria’s king will never be given this city.’

Pay no attention to Hezekiah, for the king of Assyria says: ‘Make peace with me{h} and come out to me. Then each of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree and drink water from his own cistern,

until I come and take you to a land like your own, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive trees and honey, so that you may live and not die.’ Do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you by saying, ‘Yahweh will rescue us.’
Has any of the gods of the nations ever rescued his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my hand?
Who among all the gods of the lands has rescued his land from my hand, that Yahweh should rescue Jerusalem from my hand?”
But the people kept silent and did not answer him a word, for the king’s command was, “Do not answer him.”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him what the Rabshakeh had said.

notes.text: Abi is a short form of Abijah, “Yahweh is my father” (2 Chronicles 29:1).
Nehushtan sounds like Hebrew nehosheth, “bronze,” and nahash, “serpent.” Compare Numbers 21:8–9.
Sennacherib reigned in Assyria 705–681 BC; his campaign against Judah was in 701 BC.
Hebrew “three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so about 10,200 and 1,020 kilograms.
These are Assyrian titles: Tartan, “commander in chief”; Rab-saris, “chief officer”; Rabshakeh, “chief cupbearer” or field commander.
Hebrew “in Judean.”
So the Qere; the Ketiv uses cruder words.
Hebrew “Make a blessing with me.”

verses.text: When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into Yahweh’s house.
Eliakim, who was over the household, Shebna the scribe, and the elders among the priests, dressed in sackcloth, were sent by him to the prophet Isaiah{a} son of Amoz.
They told him, “Hezekiah says this: ‘This day is one of anguish, reproof, and humiliation. The babies are at the mouth of the womb, and there is no strength to bring them out.

It may be that Yahweh your God will hear everything the Rabshakeh said, sent as he was by his lord, Assyria’s king, to taunt the living God, and will punish him for the words that Yahweh your God has heard. So lift up a prayer for the remnant that is still left.’ ”
When King Hezekiah’s servants came to Isaiah,
Isaiah told them, “Say to your master, ‘Yahweh says this: Do not be frightened by what you have heard, the words with which the lackeys of the king of Assyria have insulted me.
I am about to put a spirit in him, so that he will hear a rumor and go back to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.’ ”
The Rabshakeh went back and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had moved on from Lachish.
Then Sennacherib heard a report about Tirhakah{b} king of Cush:{c} “He has set out to fight against you.” So he again sent messengers to Hezekiah with this message:
“Say this to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Your God, in whom you trust, is fooling you when he says Jerusalem will never fall into the Assyrian king’s grip. Do not listen.
You have surely heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be rescued?
Did the gods of the nations rescue those whom my predecessors destroyed: Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?
Where now is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, or the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, or of Ivvah?’ ”
Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to Yahweh’s house and spread it out before Yahweh.
And Hezekiah prayed before Yahweh: “Yahweh, God of Israel, you who sit above the cherubim, you and you only are God of every kingdom on earth. Heaven and earth are your making.
Bend down your ear, Yahweh, and hear. Open your eyes, Yahweh, and see. Hear the words Sennacherib has sent to taunt the living God.
It is true, Yahweh, that the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands.
They have cast their gods into the flames and wiped them out, since those were no gods at all, just wood and stone that people had shaped.
Now, Yahweh our God, save us, I pray, from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, Yahweh, alone are God.”
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah: “This is what Yahweh the God of Israel says: Because you have prayed to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria, I have heard you.
This is the word Yahweh has spoken concerning him: “The virgin daughter Zion holds you in contempt and laughs you to scorn. Daughter Jerusalem tosses her head behind your back.
Whom have you taunted and reviled? Whom have you shouted at, looking down your nose so haughtily? It was Israel’s Holy One!

Through your messengers you have mocked the Lord,{d} boasting, ‘Riding at the head of my chariot host{e} I have climbed the heights of the mountains, the farthest reaches of Lebanon. I cut down its tallest cedars, its choicest junipers. I entered its most remote lodging place, its densest forest.{f}
I dug wells and drank foreign waters. Under my tramping feet every river of Egypt ran dry.’{g}
Have you not heard? Long ago I planned it. From days of old I shaped it, and now I have brought it about, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins,
while their inhabitants, drained of strength, were dismayed and put to shame. They became like plants in the field and tender green shoots, like grass on the rooftops, scorched before it grows up.{h}
But I know when you sit, when you go out and come in, and how you rage against me.
Because you have raged against me and your arrogance has reached my ears, a ring will go through your nostrils, a bridle between your lips, and I will lead you home again the way you arrived.”

“And here, Hezekiah, is your sign: for this year the food will be whatever sprouts on its own, and next year whatever comes up from that. But in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.
The survivors of the house of Judah who are left will again take root below and bear fruit above.
Out of Jerusalem a remnant will emerge, a band of escapees from Zion’s mountain. Yahweh’s{i} jealous passion will accomplish this.
Therefore this is what Yahweh says about the king of Assyria: Into this city he will not come; no arrow of his will fly over it. No shield of his will confront it, or heap up a siege ramp against it.
By the road he came, by that same road he will go back, and he will not enter this city, declares Yahweh.
I will shield this city to rescue it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.”
That very night the angel of Yahweh went out and struck down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. When the survivors{j} got up early in the morning, there were all the dead bodies.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and went home. He stayed in Nineveh.
As he bowed down in the house of Nisroch{k} his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his own sons, cut him down with swords and fled to Ararat country.{l} And Esarhaddon{m} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: Isaiah means “Yahweh is salvation.”
Tirhakah (Taharqa) was a Cushite ruler of Egypt’s Twenty-fifth Dynasty, here probably still commander of the army.
That is, the upper Nile region (modern Sudan).
Hebrew Adonai.
So the Qere and the Septuagint; the Ketiv reads “With the chariot of my chariots.”
Hebrew “the forest of its Carmel,” that is, its garden-land.
Hebrew Matsor, a poetic name for Egypt; it can also mean “siege.”
So the Hebrew; Isaiah 37:27 and some ancient witnesses read “like a terraced field.” The Hebrew phrase is uncertain.
The Septuagint reads “of Yahweh of hosts,” as in Isaiah 37:32.
Hebrew “they.”
Nisroch is otherwise unknown; it may be a corruption of Nusku or Marduk.
Ararat is Urartu, in the region of modern Armenia.
Esarhaddon reigned in Assyria 681–669 BC.

verses.text: Around that time Hezekiah fell ill and was close to dying. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “Yahweh says this: ‘Put your household in order, because you are going to die; you will not get well.’ ”
Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to Yahweh:
“Yahweh, please call to mind that I have walked in your presence with loyalty and an undivided heart and have done what is right in your eyes.” And Hezekiah broke down in tears.
Before Isaiah had got out past the middle courtyard,{a} the word of Yahweh came to him:

“Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of your ancestor David, says: I have listened to your prayer and seen your tears. I am going to heal you. Two days from now you will go up to Yahweh’s house.
I am adding fifteen years to your life. From the hand of Assyria’s king I will deliver both you and this city, and I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.’ ”
Then Isaiah said, “Bring a lump of pressed figs.” They brought it and put it on the boil, and he recovered.
Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that Yahweh is going to heal me and that I will go up to Yahweh’s house the day after tomorrow?”
Isaiah answered, “This is your sign from Yahweh that he will do what he has promised: Shall the shadow move forward ten steps{b} or go back ten steps?”
Hezekiah said, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen by ten steps. No, let the shadow turn back ten steps.”
So the prophet Isaiah called out to Yahweh, and Yahweh brought the shadow back the ten steps it had already gone down on the stairway of Ahaz.
At that time Berodach-baladan{c} son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill.

Hezekiah welcomed{d} the envoys and showed them his entire storehouse: the silver, the gold, the spices, the fine oil, his armory, and everything in his treasuries. There was nothing in his palace or anywhere in his realm that Hezekiah failed to show them.
Then the prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and asked him, “What did those men say, and where did they come from to see you?” Hezekiah replied, “They came from a distant land, from Babylon.”
Isaiah asked, “What have they seen in your palace?” Hezekiah answered, “They saw everything in my palace. Nothing among my treasures did I keep from them.”
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Listen to Yahweh’s word:
The time is surely coming when everything in your palace, and all that your ancestors have stored up to this day, will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says Yahweh.
And some of your own descendants, born from you, will be taken away, and they will serve as eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of Yahweh you have spoken is good.” For he was thinking, “Surely, then, my own days will be peaceful and secure.”

The rest of Hezekiah’s history, all his mighty deeds, and how he built the pool and the channel{e} and brought water into the city, are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Then Hezekiah lay down with his fathers, and Manasseh{f} his son became king after him.

notes.text: So the Qere and the Septuagint; the Ketiv reads “the middle city.”
Or “degrees”; Hebrew ma‘aloth, steps of a stairway used to mark time by the shadow.
Isaiah 39:1 and the Septuagint read “Merodach-baladan.” The name is Babylonian Marduk-apla-iddina, “Marduk has given an heir.”
Hebrew “listened to.” The Septuagint and Isaiah 39:2 read “rejoiced over.”
That is, the tunnel cut through rock to bring the Gihon spring’s water into the city, known today as Hezekiah’s Tunnel.
Manasseh means “causing to forget.”

verses.text: Manasseh was twelve when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem fifty-five years. His mother was named Hephzibah.{a}
He did what Yahweh considered evil, copying the detestable customs of the nations Yahweh had driven out ahead of the Israelites.

He rebuilt the shrines on the high places that his father Hezekiah had torn down. He put up altars to Baal and made an Asherah pole,{b} just as Ahab king of Israel had done, and he bowed down to the whole army of the sky and served them.
He built altars inside Yahweh’s house, the very place of which Yahweh had said, “In Jerusalem I will put my name.”
In both courtyards of Yahweh’s house he built altars for all the starry host.

He made his own son pass through the fire.{c} He practiced fortune-telling and omen reading and appointed people who consulted ghosts and familiar spirits. He did a great deal of evil in Yahweh’s eyes, provoking him to anger.

The carved image of Asherah that he had made he placed in the house about which Yahweh had told David and his son Solomon, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose out of all the tribes of Israel, I will set my name forever.

I will never again make Israel’s feet wander from the land I gave their ancestors, provided only that they take care to do all that I have commanded them, the whole law my servant Moses laid on them.”
But they would not listen. Manasseh misled them into doing more evil than the nations Yahweh had wiped out before the Israelites.
So Yahweh spoke through his servants the prophets:
“Manasseh king of Judah has committed these detestable acts, worse than anything the Amorites before him did, and with his idols{d} he has led Judah into sin as well.
Therefore this is what Yahweh the God of Israel says: I am bringing such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that both ears of everyone who hears of it will ring.

I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line used on Samaria and the plumb line used on Ahab’s house.{e} I will scour Jerusalem the way a dish is scoured, wiped out and then flipped over on its face.
What is left of my own heritage I will abandon, giving them into the power of their enemies, to be pillaged and stripped by every foe they have,
because they have done what is evil in my eyes and have gone on angering me ever since the day their fathers left Egypt, right up to today.”
What is more, Manasseh poured out the blood of the innocent in such quantity that Jerusalem was soaked with it end to end, besides the sin he led Judah into by doing evil in Yahweh’s eyes.
The rest of Manasseh’s history, all he did and the sin he committed, is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, is it not?
Manasseh lay down with his fathers and was buried in the garden of his palace, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon{f} took his place as king.
Amon was twenty-two when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem two years. His mother was Meshullemeth,{g} daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, as his father Manasseh had done.
He followed his father’s path in every way, serving and bowing down to the idols his father had served.
He turned his back on Yahweh, his fathers’ God, and refused to go in Yahweh’s way.
Amon’s own servants formed a conspiracy and murdered the king inside his house.
Then the people of the land put to death everyone who had plotted against King Amon, and they crowned Josiah,{h} Amon’s son, to succeed him.
The rest of what Amon did is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, is it not?
He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah reigned after him.

notes.text: Hephzibah means “my delight is in her.”
A wooden cult object associated with the goddess Asherah.
Some ancient witnesses, including the Septuagint, read “his sons.” The rite probably refers to child sacrifice.
The Hebrew word gillulim is a contemptuous term, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Builders’ tools, used here as an image of judgment by the same standard applied to Samaria and Ahab’s dynasty.
Amon means “faithful” or “master builder.”
Meshullemeth means “one repaid” or “one at peace.”
Josiah means “Yahweh supports.”

verses.text: Josiah was eight years old when he came to the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem thirty-one years. His mother’s name was Jedidah,{a} daughter of Adaiah, from Bozkath.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes and followed every step of his ancestor David, never veering off to right or left.
In King Josiah’s eighteenth year,{b} the king sent the secretary Shaphan{c} son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, to Yahweh’s house with these instructions:
“Go up to Hilkiah{d} the high priest and have him count out the silver brought into Yahweh’s house, which the doorkeepers have gathered from the people.
It is to be handed to the men in charge of the work on Yahweh’s house, and they are to pay it to the laborers repairing the damage to the building:
the carpenters, the builders, and the stonemasons, and to buy timber and cut stone to restore the house.
But no accounting is to be required of them for the silver given to them, for they work honestly.”
Hilkiah the high priest told Shaphan the secretary, “I have found the scroll of the law in Yahweh’s house.” Hilkiah gave the scroll to Shaphan, who read it.

Then Shaphan the secretary went to the king and gave him a report: “Your servants have emptied out the silver that was found in the house and handed it over to the men in charge of the work on Yahweh’s house.”
Then Shaphan the secretary informed the king, “There is a scroll that Hilkiah the priest handed to me.” And Shaphan read it aloud in the king’s presence.
As soon as the king heard what was written in the scroll of the law, he tore his clothes.
He gave orders to five men: Hilkiah the priest; Shaphan’s son Ahikam; Micaiah’s son Achbor;{e} Shaphan the secretary; and Asaiah, the king’s servant:

“Go and ask Yahweh on my behalf, and on behalf of the people and all Judah, about what is written in this scroll that has been found. Yahweh’s rage is burning hot against us, since our fathers never heeded what this scroll says or did all that it lays down for us.”

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to the prophetess Huldah,{f} wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem, in the Second Quarter.{g} They spoke with her,
and she said to them, “This is what Yahweh the God of Israel says: Tell the man who sent you to me,
‘Yahweh says this: I am about to bring disaster on this place and on those who live here, everything written in the scroll the king of Judah has read.
Because they have abandoned me and burned offerings to other gods, angering me with all the things their hands have made, my fury will blaze against this place and will not be put out.’
But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of Yahweh, say this: ‘Yahweh the God of Israel says this about the words you have heard:

Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before Yahweh when you heard what I spoke against this place and its inhabitants, that they would become a horror and a curse, and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I in turn have heard you, declares Yahweh.

Therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be laid in your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the disaster I am bringing on this place.’ ” And they took her answer back to the king.

notes.text: Jedidah means “beloved.”
That is, 622 BC. The Septuagint adds “in the eighth month.”
Shaphan means “rock badger.”
Hilkiah means “Yahweh is my portion.”
Achbor means “mouse.”
Huldah means “mole” or “weasel.”
Hebrew Mishneh, a newer district of Jerusalem, probably on the western hill.

verses.text: Then the king sent for all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, and they gathered around him.

The king went up to Yahweh’s house, and with him went every man of Judah, all who lived in Jerusalem, the priests and the prophets, the whole population from youngest to oldest. In their hearing he read out everything written in the scroll of the covenant that had been found in Yahweh’s house.

Standing by the pillar, the king made a covenant before Yahweh: to follow Yahweh, to keep his commands, his decrees, and his statutes with all his heart and soul, and so to carry out the terms of the covenant written in this scroll. And all the people committed themselves to the covenant.

The king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests of the second rank, and the doorkeepers to remove from Yahweh’s temple every object made for Baal, for Asherah, and for all the host of the sky. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel.

He did away with the idol priests{a} whom Judah’s kings had appointed to burn offerings at the high places in the towns of Judah and around Jerusalem, as well as those who made offerings to Baal, to sun and moon, to the star signs,{b} and to every heavenly army.
He took the Asherah from Yahweh’s house out of Jerusalem to the Kidron Valley and burned it there. He ground it to dust and scattered the dust over the graves of the common people.
He tore down the quarters of the cult prostitutes{c} that were in Yahweh’s house, where the women wove coverings{d} for Asherah.

He brought all the priests in from the towns of Judah and defiled the high places where they had burned offerings, from Geba to Beersheba.{e} He tore down the shrines of the gates{f} at the entrance of the gate of Joshua the city governor, on the left as one enters the city gate.
The priests of the high places did not go up to Yahweh’s altar in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread among their fellow priests.
Topheth{g} in the Ben-hinnom Valley he made unclean, so that nobody might ever again hand over a son or daughter to Molech by fire.

He removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance to Yahweh’s house, next to the room of Nathan-melech the official, in the colonnade,{h} and he burned the chariots of the sun.

The altars that the kings of Judah had built on the roof by Ahaz’s upper room, and the altars Manasseh had built in the two courtyards of Yahweh’s house, the king pulled down. He smashed them there{i} and threw their rubble into the Kidron Valley.

The king made unclean the high places facing Jerusalem on the east, to the right of the Mount of Ruin,{j} which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the detestable goddess of the Sidonians, for Chemosh the detestable god of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
He shattered the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled their sites with human bones.

Even the altar at Bethel, the high place set up by Jeroboam son of Nebat who made Israel sin, that altar and high place he also tore down. He burned the high place, crushed it to dust, and burned the Asherah.

As Josiah turned around, he saw the tombs there on the hillside. He sent men to take the bones out of the tombs and burned them on the altar, defiling it, in keeping with the word of Yahweh proclaimed by the man of God who had foretold these things.{k}
Then he asked, “What is this marker I see?” The men of the city answered, “It is the grave of the man of God who came from Judah and announced these very things you have done to the altar of Bethel.”
“Leave it alone,” he said. “Let no one disturb his bones.” So they left his bones undisturbed, along with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.
Josiah also removed all the shrines of the high places in the towns of Samaria that Israel’s kings had built, angering Yahweh.{l} He did to them just what he had done at Bethel.
Every priest of those high places he put to death on their own altars, and on them he burned the bones of the dead. After that he went back to Jerusalem.
The king commanded all the people, “Celebrate the Passover to Yahweh your God, as it is written in this scroll of the covenant.”
No Passover like it had been kept since the days of the judges who led Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.
But in King Josiah’s eighteenth year this Passover was celebrated to Yahweh in Jerusalem.

In addition, Josiah swept away those who called up the dead or consulted spirits, the teraphim,{m} the idols, and every loathsome thing to be seen across Judah and Jerusalem, in order to fulfill the words of the law written in the scroll Hilkiah the priest had found in Yahweh’s house.
No earlier king could compare with him in turning back to Yahweh with all his heart, soul, and might in line with the whole law of Moses, and no later king ever rose to equal him.
Even so, Yahweh did not turn from the burning heat of his great anger, which blazed against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke him.
Yahweh said, “Judah too I will remove from my sight as I removed Israel. I will reject this city I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’ ”
The rest of Josiah’s history and all he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, are they not?

In his days Pharaoh Neco{n} king of Egypt marched up to the king of Assyria{o} at the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to confront him, and the moment Neco saw him at Megiddo, he put him to death.

His servants carried his body by chariot from Megiddo, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz{p} son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in his father’s place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem three months. His mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, just as his fathers had done.
Pharaoh Neco put him in chains at Riblah in the land of Hamath to end his reign in Jerusalem,{q} and he imposed on the land a levy of about 3¾ tons of silver and about 75 pounds of gold.{r}
Eliakim, Josiah’s son, was installed by Pharaoh Neco as king to succeed Josiah his father, and Neco gave him the new name Jehoiakim.{s} Jehoahaz he carried off to Egypt, where he died.

Jehoiakim paid the silver and gold to Pharaoh, but to meet Pharaoh’s demand he had to tax the land. He exacted the silver and gold from the people of the land, from each according to his assessment, to pay Pharaoh Neco.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother was Zebidah, daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, just as his fathers had done.

verses.text: During Jehoiakim’s reign Nebuchadnezzar{a} king of Babylon came up against him, and Jehoiakim became his vassal for three years. Then he changed course and rebelled against him.

Yahweh sent raiding bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites against Jehoiakim; he let them loose on Judah to destroy it, in keeping with the word Yahweh had spoken through his servants the prophets.
Surely this came on Judah at Yahweh’s command, to thrust them out of his sight because of Manasseh’s sins, everything he had done,
and also because of the innocent blood he had shed. He had flooded Jerusalem with innocent blood, and Yahweh was not willing to forgive.
The rest of Jehoiakim’s history and all he did are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, are they not?
Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin{b} his son became king after him.
The king of Egypt did not march out of his own country again, for the king of Babylon had seized everything that had belonged to him, from the Wadi of Egypt{c} to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen when he came to the throne, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. His mother was Nehushta,{d} daughter of Elnathan, from Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the sight of Yahweh, in every way like his father before him.
It was then that the troops of Babylon’s king Nebuchadnezzar came up to Jerusalem and laid siege to the city.
Nebuchadnezzar himself arrived at the city while his officers were besieging it.

Then Jehoiachin king of Judah surrendered to the king of Babylon, he, his mother, his officials, his commanders, and his court officers. The king of Babylon took him prisoner in the eighth year of his own reign.{e}

Just as Yahweh had warned, Nebuchadnezzar hauled off all the treasures of Yahweh’s house and the palace treasures, and he stripped away the gold from all the vessels Solomon king of Israel had made for Yahweh’s temple.
He exiled all Jerusalem: all the commanders and all the leading warriors, 10,000 captives, along with every craftsman and metalworker.{f} No one was left except the poorest people of the land.
He took Jehoiachin into exile to Babylon. The king’s mother, the king’s wives, his court officers, and the leading men of the land he also led away into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.
The king of Babylon brought to Babylon as exiles all the men of valor, 7,000 of them, and 1,000 craftsmen and metalworkers, all of them strong men fit for war.
In Jehoiachin’s place the king of Babylon made his uncle{g} Mattaniah king and changed his name to Zedekiah.{h}
Zedekiah was twenty-one when he came to the throne, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother was Hamutal,{i} daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the sight of Yahweh, in every way like Jehoiakim before him.
Indeed, because of Yahweh’s anger, it came to this in Jerusalem and Judah, until he flung them away from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

verses.text: So in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month (December–January),{a} Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army. He camped outside it and built siege works all around it.
The city stayed under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year.
By the ninth day of the fourth month (June–July){b} the famine inside the city had become so severe that the common people had nothing left to eat.

Then the city wall was breached, and all the fighting men fled{c} by night through the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden, though the Chaldeans were all around the city. The king{d} headed off toward the Arabah.{e}
But the Chaldean army chased after the king and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho, and all his troops deserted him and scattered.
They seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where sentence was passed on him.
Zedekiah’s sons were slaughtered while he watched. Then Zedekiah’s eyes were put out, and he was bound in bronze shackles and taken to Babylon.

On the seventh day of the fifth month (July–August){f} (that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), Nebuzaradan,{g} commander of the guard and a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He set fire to Yahweh’s house, the palace, and every house in Jerusalem; every great house he burned down.
The whole Chaldean army that was with the commander of the guard tore down the walls surrounding Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan the commander of the guard took into exile the rest of the people still left in the city, the deserters who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the population.{h}
But the commander of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and work the fields.
The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars of Yahweh’s house, the movable stands, and the bronze Sea{i} that were in Yahweh’s house, and they carried the bronze to Babylon.
They also took the pots, the shovels, the wick trimmers, the dishes, and all the bronze utensils used in the temple service.
The commander of the guard took the firepans and the sprinkling bowls, whatever was of gold for its gold and whatever was of silver for its silver.
As for the two pillars, the one Sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for Yahweh’s house, the bronze of all these objects was beyond weighing.

Each pillar was 27 feet{j} high, with a bronze capital on top. The capital stood 4½ feet{k} high, and a latticework with pomegranates encircled the capital, all of bronze. The second pillar, with its latticework, was the same.
The commander of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three doorkeepers.

From the city he took one court official who had command of the fighting men, five members of the king’s inner circle{l} still found in the city, the secretary of the army commander,{m} who mustered the people of the land, and sixty men of the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan the commander of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them struck down and put to death. So Judah went into exile, away from its land.
Over the people who remained in the land of Judah, those whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, he appointed Gedaliah{n} son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor.

When all the army commanders and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, they came to him at Mizpah with their men. These were Nethaniah’s son Ishmael, Kareah’s son Johanan, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth from Netophah, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite.
Gedaliah swore an oath to them and their men. “Do not be afraid of the Chaldean officials,” he told them. “Settle in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well for you.”

But in the seventh month (September–October),{o} Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, who was of royal descent, came with ten men and struck Gedaliah down, killing him and also the Judeans and Chaldeans who were staying with him at Mizpah.
At that, the whole population, small and great alike, and the commanders of the troops got up and left for Egypt, fearing what the Chaldeans would do.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month (February–March),{p} Evil-merodach{q} king of Babylon, in the year he became king, released{r} Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison.
He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above the seats of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes, and for the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king’s table.
And his upkeep was supplied without fail from the king, a fixed share day by day, for as long as he lived.
